items.readable_text:
Content:
Remember that two terms are called like terms if they have the same variable part.

Content:
An expression with different terms can often be simplified by collecting like terms.

Content:
For example, consider the following expression:
[MATH: 2x+3x]

Content:
The terms [MATH: 2x] and [MATH: 3x] are like terms because they both have a variable part of [MATH: x.]

Content:
Whenever we have two or more like terms in an expression, we can combine them into a single term. Here, we can combine the like terms [MATH: 2x] and [MATH: 3x] into a single term by adding their coefficients:
[MATH: 2x + 3x|=; (2 + 3)x|=; 5x]

items.title: Rearranging an Expression Before Collecting Like Terms

sections.normalized_html:
We rearrange the terms so that the like terms, [MATH: 6a] and [MATH: -2a], are together.

[MATH: \eqalign{ 6a+1-2a &= \[5pt] \underbrace{6a-2a}_{a \textrm{ terms}}+ 1 & }]

Then, we combine the like terms:

[MATH: \eqalign{ \underbrace{6a-2a}+ 1 &= \[5pt] (6-2)a + 1 &=\[5pt] 4a + 1& }]

6a+1-2a &= \[5pt]
\underbrace{6a-2a}_{a \textrm{ terms}}+ 1	&
}]

Then, we combine the like terms:

[MATH: \eqalign{
\underbrace{6a-2a}+ 1 &= \[5pt]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we group the like terms. [MATH: \eqalign{ 2.5x+2y-x+1.5y &= \[5pt] \underbrace{2.5x-x}_{x \textrm{ terms}}+\underbrace{2y+1.5y}_{y \textrm{ terms}} & }]

Then, we combine the like terms: [MATH: \eqalign{ \underbrace{2.5x-x}+\underbrace{2y+1.5y} &= \[5pt] (2.5-1)x + (2+1.5)y &=\[5pt] 1.5x + 3.5y }]

items.readable_text:
Example Prompt:
Simplify the expression [MATH: 2.5x+2y-x+1.5y.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we group the like terms.
[MATH: \eqalign{
2.5x+2y-x+1.5y &= \[5pt]
\underbrace{2.5x-x}_{x \textrm{ terms}}+\underbrace{2y+1.5y}_{y \textrm{ terms}} &
}]

Then, we combine the like terms:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\underbrace{2.5x-x}+\underbrace{2y+1.5y} &= \[5pt]
(2.5-1)x + (2+1.5)y &=\[5pt]
1.5x + 3.5y
}]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Remember that two terms are called like terms if they have the same variable part.

Content:
An expression with different terms can often be simplified by collecting like terms.

Content:
For example, consider the following expression:
[MATH: 2x+3x]

Content:
The terms [MATH: 2x] and [MATH: 3x] are like terms because they both have a variable part of [MATH: x.]

Content:
Whenever we have two or more like terms in an expression, we can combine them into a single term. Here, we can combine the like terms [MATH: 2x] and [MATH: 3x] into a single term by adding their coefficients:
[MATH: 2x + 3x|=; (2 + 3)x|=; 5x]

---

Item 2 — Example: Simplifying Expressions With Two or Three Terms

Example Prompt:
Simplify the expression [MATH: 2 + 7p - 3p.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We have two like terms, [MATH: 7p] and [MATH: -3p.]

To collect these like terms, we combine them into a single term, adding their coefficients:

[MATH: 2 + 7p − 3p|=; 2 + (7 − 3)p|=; 2 + 4p]

6a+1-2a &= \[5pt]
\underbrace{6a-2a}_{a \textrm{ terms}}+ 1	&
}]

\underbrace{6a-2a}+ 1 &= \[5pt]

2.5x+2y-x+1.5y &= \[5pt]
\underbrace{2.5x-x}_{x \textrm{ terms}}+\underbrace{2y+1.5y}_{y \textrm{ terms}} &
}]

Then, we combine the like terms:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\underbrace{2.5x-x}+\underbrace{2y+1.5y} &= \[5pt]
(2.5-1)x + (2+1.5)y &=\[5pt]
1.5x + 3.5y
}]
